events.title: The Axios founders on how AI ruined your inbox, why the ’90s really were different and how to succeed through ‘Simplify’
events.summary: Three years after Smart Brevity became gospel inside corporate comms departments, the founders of Axios are back with a diagnosis of what broke their own prescription: artificial intelligence. Jim VandeHei, Mike Allen and Roy Schwartz sat down with Fortune to talk about their new book, Simplify: Do 50% More with 50% Less , out this month. The pitch: AI hasn’t lightened anyone’s workload so far—it’s flooded offices with more decks, longer emails and more “work-like activity” that produces motion without progress. Their fix is a framework the trio says they built by testing it on themselves first. How AI ruined your inbox The argument is a familiar one amid the “AI slop” discourse of 2026: the technology sold as an efficiency unlock has, in the short run, made everything worse. “When I talk to people at corporations, they’re like, ‘My team is drowning, everyone thinks they’re smart now,” VandeHei said, adding that it’s a “real issue” with how many people who never made a deck or presentation before are suddenly generating things that need an exhaustive review. At the same time, incoming pitches have all multiplied, Allen added, both inside companies and in how they present themselves externally—a two-front squeeze, not just an internal one. “Everybody’s more verbose,” Allen said, chalking it up to human nature. “Left to our own devices, we’re going to complexify,” Allen said. “Our meetings stack up, our habits, all our time sucks, and unless you are ruthless about auditing, confronting, looking at what you can delete, then [you won’t feel] the liberation of having more.” Allen borrowed a phrase from former Slack CEO Stewart Butterfield to describe the trap of “work-like activity,” which McKinsey partner Kate Smaje previously told Fortune is like a “false productivity trap.” The two run together in most organizations, Allen said, and that’s precisely the problem. VandeHei pushed back on the idea that humans are lazy by nature, a common criticism of the “cognitive offloading” enabled by AI. “People are not being lazy or stupid,” he said—they want to work hard but are having trouble right now distinguishing from real work and work-like activity, further clouded by AI. “It just creates this, like, energy and life of its own that has no meaning. It does not help.” He said they decided to write this book because of this “freaky” current moment in AI: “Everyone’s going to be scrambling, like, ‘How do I do this? How do I navigate this?'” He argued that most companies have been “very, very clumsy” in implementing it: Even if it’s amazing, which I think the technology often is, the minute you introduce it into a company and its process, its data pool, its privacy laws, its security systems,” he trailed off, “it’s just womp womp.” Their proposed remedy is a recurring audit, done more often than most companies are used to. VandeHei used to run this exercise quarterly; now he says he’s trying monthly, and flirted with a weekly cadence in conversation with Fortune . “What are the things you actually need to be doing in one order? What are the things that you can stop doing? What are the things that you can automate?” he said. “That’s basically what every company is going to have to go through.” A companion column Allen published on Axios lays out the stakes in raw hours: of 168 hours in a week, sleep and work eat up roughly 90 to 100, and the authors cite Harvard research suggesting people spend half of what remains thinking about things unrelated to what they’re doing—leaving most people in control of only “about one-sixth” of their own lives. The power of ‘I’m booked’ Allen, a famously private person, as captured by a Mark Leibovich profile in 2010 for The New York Times Magazine , described how he’s implemented the “simplify” tenets to his own personal life: “two words that we teach people are, ‘I’m booked.’ Anytime somebody wants you to do something, join something, you don’t have to apologize, you don’t have to explain, just say, ‘I’m booked.'” Allen reflected back to earlier in his career: “So many of us coming up thought that we had to hang out and do all that stuff, and it turns out, you don’t.” The book’s actual instruction, he said, is almost comically simple: if your gut response to an invitation is “eh, I probably should, I guess so, whatever”—that’s a no. He said that as he, VandeHei and Schwartz talked to successful people for this book, “it was surprising how many of them said, ‘I never accept any obligation that’s not family or work.'” On the flipside if you commit to something, really commit to being there, and then it will be worth your time. He invoked a favorite saying of Oprah Winfrey’s: “ no is a complete sentence .” VandeHei said the phrase reflects a broader refusal to separate his work and personal obligations into different systems. “I don’t know how people distinguish between work and life. To me they’re just life. And work’s a part of it,” he said. Schwartz, the third head of the Axios trifecta and an unlikely near-20-year veteran of journalism, said the real breakthrough for him wasn’t the phrase itself but the guilt it’s designed to erase. VandeHei and Allen hired Schwartz from Gallup in 2008 and roughly a year later he became chief revenue officer, a move they credit with transforming Politico’s model before they co-founded Axios together in 2016. Schwartz helped lead Axios through its funding rounds and its $525 million acquisition by Cox Enterprises and now runs Axios HQ, the company’s AI-powered internal-communications spinoff, which recently turned profitable on roughly $20 million in annualized revenue. He ties the milestone to the same simplification principles laid out in the book. His personal thread in Simplify centers on dyslexia, which he says became the root of his instinct for distilling complicated material into simple, structured points. Even after living by the book’s principles at work and at home, Schwartz said, he kept feeling guilty about declining opportunities he hadn’t formally ruled out. “What was really clarifying is when you set down the goals and you put them in writing… it actually gives you permission,” he said. “I had sort of done that mental map. I had my goals. But I still had the guilt feeling of like, ‘No, I should be doing everything.’ And the reality is you can’t do everything. So then do the things that m

events.title: My first law firm billed clients $600 per hour for me to use my Harvard degree on data entry. Thank God AI is changing the industry
events.summary: When I was 12 years old, I walked into the district attorney’s office of my Kansas hometown and asked for a job. I was inspired by onscreen lawyers depicted as hardworking professionals fighting for the rights of others or strategizing the best way to pull off a multibillion transaction. Despite the advice of everyone in the profession, I spent my entire adolescence and young adulthood preparing to become a lawyer. I was ecstatic when I was accepted and then graduated from Harvard Law School. I had spent more than a decade envisioning all that I’d do with my law degree. My first task at a law firm was to manually ensure signature lines were the same length across 18 different documents set. The firm billed the client over $600 an hour for me to use all of my schooling and education to accomplish this task.  It’s been commonly accepted that American corporations and individuals pay for young associates with prestigious credentials an alarmingly high billable hour to complete non-legal tasks. That is no longer the case. The legal profession I entered upon graduation is already dramatically different. Whether the industry likes it or not, the introduction of artificial intelligence is reshaping the distribution of talent and availability of resources, which I ultimately think will be beneficial to lawyers and clients alike.  The use of AI in white-collar professions is still in its infancy. Lawyers complain about hallucinations, mistakes, and the technology’s other shortcomings. But despite its imperfections, AI is already transforming the way that most people practice law.  Harvey and Legora first entered the scene less than five years ago and have catalyzed the change. The two dominate the BigLaw AI scene, acting more like tech companies than law companies as they sponsor sports leagues, plaster celebrity spokespeople on billboards, and hold multibillion valuations ($15 and $5.6 billion, respectively). It used to be a running joke that selling legal tech was near-impossible because law partners have no incentive to maximize efficiency and no desire to re-learn their expensive, prestigious skillsets. Now, legal tech is the hottest thing in Silicon Valley. BigLaw firms are spending to hire top-name engineers and transforming themselves into tech companies behind the scenes. The convergence of law and the tech world was unimaginable when I was in law school. As law firms are forced to adjust their models, their leaders are also reconsidering their place in the industry.  Lawyers are realizing they no longer need a big firm’s infrastructure or training model, and star players are walking out of top firms and taking their books of business with them. Chris Kercher leaving Quinn Emanuel to launch a small, tech-driven firm isn’t an outlier. He’s just early. Technology will transform the legal industry much how the internet transformed search.  A decade from now, many BigLaw firms will be skeletons of themselves.  Along the way, access to high-quality legal will expand dramatically.  As AI allows for the proliferation of knowledge and access to resources, this will democratize access to high quality legal and flatten the influence of major law firms—and the inherent advantage held by the small number of clients currently able to afford their services. Lawyers also have enormous upside. Whereas they have historically been funneled into hierarchical law firms to spend a couple years billing time around the clock for no profit share, there are already countless more ways for young attorneys to leverage their degrees and skills. It’s an incredibly exciting time to be a lawyer. We are practicing in an era of transformation, as a previously guarded industry is opening up to the masses in real time. At the AI-powered law firm that I run, we see hundreds of applications every day from the brightest students wanting to take part in that shift. events.title: How Iraq’s first digital bank is reshaping cash-driven economy
events.summary: When Kawa Junad began building Iraq 's first digital bank, the biggest challenge was not technology. It was persuading Iraqis of the value of banking itself when most of them had never needed one. For Mr Junad, the founder of First Iraqi Bank, that meant tackling what he calls a “chicken and egg” problem: customers needed merchants to accept digital payments, but merchants needed customers before they had a reason to make the switch. “It was a rough first six months or so as we pushed against all those elements, going door to door with both merchants and consumers,” Mr Junad told The National . Eventually, he built a base of about 3,000 small and medium-sized businesses able to trade through the app by late 2021, several months after FIB launched its digital application in April that year. “That proved to be the tipping point, and it’s been steady growth from there,” he said. FIB’s rise from a digital banking start-up to more than a million customers indicates how Iraq’s traditionally cash-based economy is changing as younger consumers and SMEs increasingly embrace digital payments. The bank's journey from the early challenge of building a customer and merchant ecosystem to expanding into financial services also reflects a broader transformation in Iraq’s banking sector as regulators push for stronger compliance, greater financial inclusion and modern services. FIB is a privately held Iraqi Islamic bank, which as been licensed by the Central Bank of Iraq since 2020, and operates primarily through a digital and mobile banking model. It initially built its presence in the Kurdistan region after launching its digital application in April 2021, before widening its focus to other major population centres, including Baghdad, Basra, Najaf and Nineveh. Despite being a digital-only institution, the bank is using physical branches as part of that expansion strategy. "I enjoy the irony here," Mr Junad said. “Having that anchor, that physical presence you can look at, see, go into and touch, if need be, opens many people’s willingness to give us a try – and once they do, they’re hooked.” FIB was built to eliminate obstacles to formal banking by offering streamlined onboarding, digital ID solutions, and payment tools. Using automated account opening, customers can establish a live account using a mobile phone and one or two identification documents in about five minutes. It now has about 1.3 million registered customers, 90 per cent of whom had not previously held a bank account and instead relied mainly on cash, he said. Around 30,000 merchants are using its services, allowing businesses to accept payments through smartphones without investing in additional point-of-sale equipment, he added. “This shows how hungry the market is for technologies that actually make life easier,” Mr Junad said. This growth has increasingly been driven by one of the simplest digital tools: QR payments, he added. To illustrate that hunger, he said digital payment transactions through FIB had increased by more than 85 per cent from 2024 to 2025 and by more than 70 per cent in the first half of 2026. He did not provide the underlying transaction volumes or values. For thousands of SMEs, the change has been particularly visible. He said some businesses using the bank's QR services have moved from almost entirely cash transactions to receiving only about 20 per cent of their payments in cash. The bank’s evolution has gone beyond payments. Mr Junad added that about 30 per cent of its customer base now uses services such as savings, credit and salary accounts. That transition is significant because it points to the next stage of Iraq’s digital banking experiment: moving customers from digital payments to deeper relationships with the banking system. The next step, he says, is to turn that digital relationship into access to credit. “We expect digital lending and credit to become a meaningful part of FIB’s business,” he said, predicting significant progress by the end of 2026 or early 2027, particularly for SMEs and customers who have historically had limited access to formal credit. That would represent a much bigger change than simply making payments digital. It could give businesses that have operated largely in cash a pathway towards formal borrowing, while giving banks more data to assess customers. This is a game-changer in the near-term, and not a far-off hope FIB founder Kawa Junad Younger generation's impact The change is particularly visible among younger Iraqis, who are increasingly encountering banking through their phones rather than through a branch. For this generation, a banking service can mean paying a bill in a few taps, scanning a QR code at a shop or sending money without handling cash, while longer-term savings and investment products remain less developed, he said. Most new customers have been aged between 18 and 35, with FIB estimating total new customer acquisitions at 600 billion to 700 billion Iraqi dinars (about $500 million) a month, Mr Junad said. Transactions have increased by 5 per cent month-on-month this year, with the vast majority involving the younger generation, he added. Iraq's population grew from about 25 million in 2003 to about 46 million in 2024, when the last census was held. About 60 per cent of Iraqis are between 15 and 64 years old and around 36 per cent are below 15, the census showed. As part of reforms, the Central Bank of Iraq issued new digital banking regulations in 2024 to provide the necessary structure for a rapidly growing marketplace. Last year, the central bank licensed several digital banks that are still being established. Mr Junad described the shift brought by digital banking as a “game-changer in the near term, and not a far-off hope” for an economy where informal cash transactions remain widespread.

events.title: I’m a KPMG forward-deployed engineer. AI has moved my job beyond writing code.
events.summary: KPMG's Justin Johnsen has been an FDE at the firm for over a year now. KPMG Justin Johnsen started at KPMG in 2020 as a federal Salesforce developer, writing code by hand. Over the past year, he switched into a new role as a forward-deployed engineer at KPMG. His work involves giving AI applications the right context and coaching clients on how to use them. This is a conversation with Justin Johnsen, the lead technical architect at KPMG. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity. I joined KPMG six years ago, and I've been a forward-deployed engineer for about a year, working across different clients. When I started with KPMG as a software engineer , all the code was written by hand. I studied computer science. I built my career in architecture and later got into consulting and client work. A forward-deployed engineer works directly with a client and stays with the problem from understanding the business need through delivering a working solution. We work directly with client teams, often on-site. A lot of what I do now is AI. AI is incredibly capable, but it's really only as good as its context. Much of my work is gathering the information needed for AI to generate valuable assets and artifacts, then spreading those outputs across client deliverables and software applications. I also coach client teams on how to use AI effectively — helping them combine technical depth, business understanding, and clear communication to improve and amplify their work. For one client, I was initially hired to integrate several applications into a complex software system. After months of gathering requirements and refining the context, we used AI to deliver the application in about a month. The client wanted to understand how we had moved so quickly — and why the process had been so transparent. The client then asked me to help its teams adopt the AI and prompting practices that had made the work possible. AI has made it easier for me to multiply my output and, in a sense, act as my own enterprise. I can maintain context across multiple clients and projects simultaneously. The bottleneck used to be software development and writing code ; now it is gathering context and refining intent before development begins. One recent application I delivered involved risk scoring: using AI to assess how risky a customer or partner might be for a client to do business with. We brought together the signals used to measure that risk, then used AI to reason across them and generate a score. Independent reviewers could then use that AI-generated score in their assessments. A pattern I've noticed is that more software-development work is moving toward the data and integration layers. Many enterprise challenges come down to helping AI make sense of data, bringing information together for monitoring and visibility, and deriving value from data spread across legacy and cloud applications . Much of my work involves aggregating large volumes of data, using AI to reason over it, and connecting systems that do not naturally communicate with one another. Being on-site has real advantages. Conversations happen organically, and it is easier to read body language and emotions in person than over Teams. Some clients are remote , but when teams are in the office, I am usually there too. A forward-deployed engineer offers more than a traditional software handoff. In a conventional implementation, a systems integrator may gather requirements, build the software, and hand it back to the client. That can create a "throw it over the wall" dynamic. I have seen plenty of mangled Salesforce implementations . By working directly with client teams while developing, training, and coaching, I can transfer knowledge in real time. The client receives the application, along with the best practices, documentation, and artifacts needed to adopt it. AI gives me more space to define problems and make critical decisions instead of spending that time on repeatable, monotonous tasks. I can focus more on the things that require human judgment. events.title: This Ford exec put her family's Claude assistant on a PIP. ChatGPT has taken over.
events.summary: This mom vibe coded a family chief of staff. She's switching agents and putting the OG on a PIP. Whitney Stefko Dover Three months ago, Whitney Stefko Dover told BI about her Claude-built family chief of staff. The agent is on a PIP. An OpenAI agent has assumed the responsibilities. "The power of being a user is this constant iteration," she said. Claudette is on a performance improvement plan. Three months ago, Whitney Stefko Dover, a director and senior counsel of policy and legal operations at Ford, told Business Insider that she had vibe coded her family a chief of staff using a bespoke Claude assistant named Claudette. The agent turned her family's emails and calendars into a 4 a.m. briefing called the "Daily Dover." It was an early morning email that organized school schedules, childcare coverage, travel, birthdays, and household chores. It also drafted a useful morning text for her husband, Chris Dover. Claudette "probably saved our marriage," she previously said. Now, there's fresh competition for the chief of staff role — but Claudette hasn't been fully fired. Yet. "I'm not convinced that, like, next month, Claudette won't be the superior chief of staff," Stefko Dover told Business Insider. "She's on a PIP." Now, Gigi, a chief of staff she built in ChatGPT Work, is the fresh-faced agent parsing through the Dover family calendar. Stefko Dover says her husband, a longtime OpenAI user, encouraged her to try ChatGPT. An August Substack post from Silicon Valley venture capital firm A16z gave her another push to try new agents. "Turns out I have a lot of tool bias, which was unexpected," she said about her reluctance to abandon Claudette after months of refining. For her family, Gigi offered a better interface, maintained more continuity across projects, and produced stronger first drafts of emails and PowerPoint presentations, Stefko Dover said. It also made more proactive suggestions without waiting to be prompted. And the switch to ChatGPT was surprisingly painless. Stefko Dover had previously created a guide explaining how the assistant worked and connected with her family's apps. She uploaded that material into ChatGPT, bringing much of the old assistant's context with it. "I think kind of the key here is owning your context, right?" she said. "I think it is our job as the users to sort of own the context layer." Since the switch, Gigi has taken on even more responsibilities, Stefko Dover said. Every Friday, it reads a grocery list shared with the family's nanny and fills online shopping carts. Stefko Dover still reviews and pays for the order herself, because it still needs some supervision. "If I were to do that, I'd probably get, like, a $500 credit card limit so that there wasn't, like, Gigi purchasing diamonds on Rodeo Drive," she said when asked if she'd give her agent purchasing power. At one point, it suggested that her husband send flowers to his best friend's wife after mistaking her for a relative . A grocery haul recommendation included 12 boxes of bow-tie pasta. Still, Stefko Dover said it makes fewer contextual errors than Claudette and remembers more about the different parts of her identity. She told Business Insider that Gigi shouldn't expect to have the job forever. "There's not a final destination here," she said. "The power of being a user is this constant iteration." She wasn't kidding. Since the interview, Stefko Dover said she has added a third assistant to the family's AI org chart: Ingrid, built with the buzzy, invite-only Instinct AI , which can carry out tasks through text messages and phone calls. "I'm layering Ingrid on top of Gigi," she said. "Example: Instead of me sending Chris a text message with to-dos, it can just talk to his agent (since we've both activated this capability), and his agent can then go perform tasks on his behalf!" events.title: Dementia care can cost a fortune. Families pay in more ways than one.
events.summary: Angela Davis, 65, has cared for her mother with dementia for the past few years. Camille Farrah Lenain for BI When Angela Davis discovered that her mother with dementia had changed the locks, she knew she had to intervene. After a standard care facility didn't cut it, Davis, 65, moved her mother into her own home. Davis now manages her medications, assists with her hygiene, and monitors her at night. She sleeps on a love seat near her mom's room in case anything happens. Her mom's care, plus home maintenance , has cost about $7,000 a month. Her mom receives $3,200 monthly in retirement income , and Davis covers the rest. The stress has weighed her down; last week, she took what she thought would be a short evening nap. Next thing she knew, it was 7 a.m. the next morning and time to go to work. Angela Davis said caring for her mother with dementia has weighed her down. Camille Farrah Lenain for BI "It's death by 1,000 cuts, and in this case, you could say death by 1,000 memories every day," Davis said. Seven million Americans have Alzheimer's, leaving families to navigate rising costs for memory care facilities or home care. One estimate shows that lifetime costs for dementia can exceed $400,000. Two dozen families navigating dementia care told Business Insider that costs add up for frequent hospitalizations and physician visits, expensive medications, transportation costs, and round-the-clock home care. Those who can afford it spend five figures on monthly memory care facility costs. Other costs included home modifications, power-of-attorney legal fees, and technologies for aging in place . Are you paying for your own or your loved one's long-term care? Do you have thoughts to share about long-term care in the US? To share your story with a reporter, please fill out this quick form . A report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that in 2025, one in four family caregivers cared for someone 50 and over with memory issues or dementia. While an estimated 7 million Americans aged 65 and over have Alzheimer's, that is expected to surge. Wendy Rowland, 53, has cared for her husband with early onset Lewy body dementia for years. To manage his treatment, they spent through his 401(k) and sold their house of 20 years, then put him into a memory care facility two years ago that now costs $6,750 a month. "I hope nothing like that happens with me, and if it does, I don't know if I would want anybody else to go through the same thing of having to figure out what to do," Rowland said. The cost of memory care can be steep It pained Keith Pavlick, 53, to witness his father slowly forget his family members' names and lose track of his surroundings. He hadn't fully anticipated the financial hit that came with it. Pavlick, a real estate agent in Orlando, has helped his mother, 79, and his father, 80, since his dementia diagnosis in March 2025. His parents moved into an assisted living facility for $9,000 a month. The $9,000 is just the start, Pavlick told Business Insider earlier this year. He knows his dad will need a heightened level of care, and memory care facilities in his area cost $14,000 monthly. "Unless you're starting out investing or bought SpaceX at the IPO, then you're probably not going to be able to take care of your parents when they're that age by yourself," Pavlick said. "I'm probably going to be selling real estate until I'm dead." Keith Pavlick helped his parents move into an assisted living facility. Courtesy of Keith Pavlick Memory care costs a median of about $8,000 monthly, according to data from SeniorLiving.org. They're more expensive than standard assisted living centers because dementia patients require 24/7 supervision by specialized caregivers. They also have high security and maintenance costs. Medicare generally doesn't fund long-term memory care. Medicaid chips in for eligible families, though many said they have paid out of pocket or used long-term care insurance . Sharon Winterton, 53, has juggled working a tech sales job, raising a 14-year-old daughter, and caring for her 90-year-old mother with vascular dementia. Winterton moved her mom into an independent living facility as her memory declined. Her mom had invested in long-term care insurance, which she's used to cover her $7,000 monthly assisted living costs. Winterton said they're fortunate to avoid the high out-of-pocket cost, though she's splurged on technologies that allow her to change TV channels and monitor her mom remotely. "Thankfully, I don't have to worry a lot about her long-term care," Winterton said. There are many costs beyond direct care itself Jenn Verser, 45, hadn't anticipated moving into her childhood home in New Jersey to help care for her dad with Alzheimer's. Verser is selling her home and planning to build a two-story, roughly 1,000-square-foot addition to her parents' house . She expects it will cost at least $600,000, which they're planning to cover with a home equity line of credit, her parents' investment accounts, and the sale of her home. She said it's important to get started as quickly as possible, so that her dad can get familiar and comfortable with the addition as his Alzheimer's progresses and confusion increases. Her parents will be moving into the addition, which is "elder-friendly," with the goal of aging in place. Verser, her husband, and her child will move into the main area. Though some families told Business Insider they avoided memory care in favor of at-home care , the costs are often comparable. Tatyana Zlotsky, CEO of A Place for Mom, a platform connecting senior care providers and families, said that with home care costing about $30 an hour, based on the platform's internal data, this can end up being over $250,000 a year for 24/7 care. Angela Davis said her mom's care has been pricey. Camille Farrah Lenain for BI An early retirement or remote job can help caregivers minimize costs. Families have invested thousands of dollars in age-tech designed for dementia care, such as motion-sensor cameras, medication monitoring, and smart home devices like stove shut-off devices. Others have spent five figures on home renovations for their loved ones. Ann Gynn, 55, had cared for her mom until September, when she moved into memory care. In 2024, the content marketer in Cleveland started using JubileeTV, a remote caregiving platform allowing for remote monitoring through the TV, after many frustrating back-and-forth phone calls with her mom. Gynn created a schedule of her mom's favorite shows, and she sometimes uses the drop-in feature to see which nursing aides are in the room. "It gives me peace of mind that I have ways to get in touch with her and ways to help her that I don't physically have to be there for," Gynn said. Emotional costs can be a heavy burden too For many families, the greatest cost of dementia care isn't financial. events.title: The CEO who leads one handwritten note at a time
events.summary: Twilio CEO Khozema Shipchandler in June at the Nasdaq, celebrating the company's 10th anniversary since its IPO NYSE: TWLO Twilio CEO Khozema Shipchandler writes notes to his company's 80+ leaders before their annual retreat. He said the analog ritual is rooted in part in his own memories of being a junior employee at GE. The notes also help him build relationships with those who could one day sit in Twilio's C-suite, he said. At least once a year, Twilio CEO Khozema Shipchandler's right hand cramps up from a few hours of writing. He's not signing copies of a book. The pain, instead, comes from penning personalized notes to every member of the technology company's 80-plus-person leadership team ahead of their annual retreat . "After every 10, I have to take a 30-minute break," Shipchandler told Business Insider of the deliberately analog ritual, which is rooted partly in his own memories of being a more junior employee at GE and how special it felt to have a senior leader take notice of him. "I have no idea what the words were, I can't remember, but I definitely remember how I felt when that happened," said Shipchandler. "If I can do that just for one person and it increases their confidence or their capacity or their desire to go do a hard thing, I think that's pretty awesome," he said. Shipchandler, 52, added that the notes serve another purpose: helping him build relationships with people who could one day sit in Twilio's C-suite. He said they typically include a mention of a project or initiative the leader is driving; something complimentary about their leadership style; and encouragement for what's next. "At some point I'm going to retire, and there's a new generation of people that I want to know intimately and that I want to know to know me intimately," Shipchandler said. "They are our bench." 'They're owed information' Founded in 2008, Twilio provides technology that businesses use to interact with customers over phone calls, texts, and emails. Shipchandler rose to the top job at the company in 2024 — his first stint as CEO — after serving as president of communications and, before that, as operating chief and as finance chief. He spent 22 years at GE prior to joining Twilio in 2018. Shipchandler's handwritten notes offer a window into his broader approach to leadership. He said he's committed to responding to employees' emails, texts, and Slack messages within 24 to 48 hours and that he makes a habit of reading meeting materials in advance to respect participants' time. He also said he aims to be a "straight shooter" rather than a CEO who papers over hard news with "corporate speak." "My style is to be as transparent as I possibly can be," he said. "I do that because I think everyone — whether it's an employee or an investor or the board — they're owed information that they can make decisions about." The next generation of leaders Shipchandler oversees a roughly 5,500-person workforce with optional in-office attendance, a stance increasingly at odds with policies at other large employers , many of which have brought back white-collar workers at least part-time. He said Twilio's remote-friendly model has held up on the metrics that matter to him: Productivity remained steady after the company went remote during the pandemic, while recruiting, engagement, and retention improved. The arrangement has made it harder, though, to foster culture . "We recognize there are downsides," said Shipchandler, which is why he added that Twilio creates deliberate opportunities for employees to build relationships in person. These include periodic paid trips for team get-togethers and free lunch on Thursdays at the company's San Francisco headquarters. Shipchandler has also taken a contrarian view of middle managers compared with some of Twilio's tech peers. Rather than trim their ranks and have those who remain rely more on AI, as companies including Block and Meta have done, he said that Twilio is continuing to invest in the midlevel cohort through training programs. Twilio's next generation of senior leaders could come from this group, he said, and managers bring something AI lacks. "The thing that's hard to replace is judgment," said Shipchandler. "That's what the managers do." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Asian Games: Smriti Mandhana breaks T20 record as India beat Bangladesh
events.summary: India defeat Bangladesh by 114 runs to book women’s cricket final against Sri Lanka, who beat Pakistan by eight wickets. Smriti Mandhana has become the highest run-scorer in women’s T20 international cricket, guiding India to a crushing win over Bangladesh in an Asian Games semifinal in Japan. The recently crowned Asian champions defeated Bangladesh by 114 runs on Sunday as Mandhana’s fellow opener Shafali Verma hit her maiden T20 hundred at the Korogi Athletic Park ground in Nagoya. Mandhana scored 37 off 19 balls with five fours and two sixes in her side’s 195-4 in 20 overs and, in the process, went past New Zealand all-rounder Suzie Bates’s 4,758 runs at the top of the all-time list to stand on 4,788 runs from 171 innings. Earlier this month, Mandhana reached the top of overall run-scoring charts in women’s international cricket after smashing a record-breaking 124 off 64 balls in the Women’s Asia Cup in Dubai. Mandhana overtook former India captain Mithali Raj , who had been the top international scorer with 10,868 international runs, during her match-winning innings against Hong Kong on Thursday. Verma was the star on the day for India in the Asian Games semifinal, scoring 100 not out off 49 balls with three fours and nine sixes. She reached her hundred off the final ball of the 20-over innings and was clearly emotional as she took off her helmet and raised her bat in celebration towards her applauding teammates on the boundary. India then restricted Bangladesh to 81 in 15.4 overs. The 50-over world champions will meet Sri Lanka on Tuesday in the gold medal match, which will be a replay of the Asia Cup final from last Sunday, when India won a record-extending eighth title. Sri Lanka advanced to the final after their captain Chamari Athapaththu led them to an easy eight-wicket win over Pakistan with more than two overs to spare. The island nation hunted down the 178-run target with 13 balls to spare as Athapaththu led the scoring with 83 not out. Earlier, Pakistan were asked to bat first and, with half-centuries from Ayesha Zafar and Shawaal Zulfiqar, they posted a total of 177-4 in 20 overs. Zafar, who hit the joint third-fastest fifty for Pakistan in WT20Is off 27 balls, shared a record stand of 115 with Zulfiqar, which is the second-highest in the format for Pakistan and the highest for the third wicket. Pakistan were able to score 27 runs off the last three overs as their all-rounder captain Fatima Sana hit two fours and one six in her 12-ball 20. In reply, Sana broke Sri Lanka’s 36-run opening stand in the fifth over, bowling out Imesha Dulani for 27. Athapaththu, who hit seven fours and six sixes in her 50-ball knock, joined forces with Hasini Perera (42) to form a match-winning 95-run partnership off 56 balls. Nashra Sundhu provided Pakistan the breakthrough in the 14th over, with Sri Lanka requiring another 47 runs off the last six overs, but Athapaththu’s quickfire stand of 47 off 23 balls with Harshitha Samrawickrama (17 not out) took their team over the line with 13 balls to spare. Pakistan will play Bangladesh for the bronze medal, also on Tuesday.

events.title: A Lyft driver was in a crash on the job. Now he's struggling to provide — and fighting insurance.
events.summary: Osahon Aburime, a former Lyft driver, was injured in a car accident. Osahon Aburime A Lyft driver in North Carolina was involved in an accident while en route to pick up a passenger. Sixteen months later, he's still fighting for an insurance payout. He said that accident has also made it harder to support his family. Osahon Aburime opened his Lyft app on Mother's Day last year to make some money. That day, the North Carolina driver had made about $80 to put toward taking his wife out to dinner and getting a gift for his mom. As he was on his way to pick up a passenger, though, he got into a car accident. "All of a sudden, I just saw this car in front of me, so I stepped on my brakes," he said. "We just ran into each other." Sixteen months later, he uses a cane to walk, he said. He tried unsuccessfully to return to work as a ride-hailing driver. "I said, 'Let me see if I can continue to drive to make money for my family,'" he said. "But it just got to a point now I can't even bend down." Aburime's experience shows one occupational hazard of working as a driver for a gig-work platform like Lyft or Uber. While the apps say they provide insurance coverage, the independent contractors doing the work often have fewer protections than traditional full-time employees. "Safety is fundamental to Lyft and it is our goal to make every ride safe, comfortable and reliable," a Lyft spokesperson said. "We maintain auto liability insurance that meets local and state regulations." 'Nobody deserves this' After the accident, Aburime had pain in one of his feet, according to a report from the hospital viewed by Business Insider. He also lost the Chevy Malibu that he was driving when he got into the accident. His income has also been affected. Before the accident, it was typical for him to make around $1,700 a month on Lyft. The money helped support his family, along with his wife's income working at an eye clinic. Since the accident, though, he hasn't been able to earn money, he said. That led him to fall behind on payments toward his minivan, which his lender repossessed earlier this year, according to a notice seen by Business Insider. Aburime has also been fighting to get a payout from Mobilitas, which provides ride-hailing insurance to Lyft. Aburime said that he's reached out to the North Carolina Department of Insurance for help. The department has told him to look for a lawyer — something he says he can't afford. A day after the accident, Mobilitas denied Aburime's claim, according to the insurance documents he provided. The denial contained incorrect information about the accident, though, including the wrong time, according to a letter sent from North Carolina's insurance department . It also suggested that Aburime wasn't on his way to pick up a passenger when the accident happened — something he denies. The company has since corrected some of the details, but has continued to deny his claim. Mobilitas did not respond to a request for comment on this story. Fighting for an insurance payout has taken time away from trying to find other work and recovering from his injuries, he said. "These rideshare companies tell you that you are covered if something like this happens," he said. Other gig workers have faced their own challenges after suddenly not being able to work on apps like Uber and Instacart. In some cases, the companies have deactivated workers' accounts , Business Insider previously reported. The company's policies say that workers can lose access to the apps by abusing them. Some drivers have told Business Insider that they were kicked off the apps — and lost income — after an overcharge at a store checkout. One Instacart worker won $28,000 in back pay after a months-long arbitration process over such a deactivation. Others, like Aburime, have tried to get insurance settlements after getting injured on a gig. "I don't think any company should treat the people who work with them like this," Aburime said. events.title: Meet a 71-year-old who retired as a radiologist and professor, and now runs a banana-skewer business: ‘I never want to retire. Why would you do that?’
events.summary: At 71, Richard Brown feels as if he’s a college student all over again. A nuclear medicine physician turned professor, Brown formally retired in 2020—only to take another job in university leadership the following week and join a venture-backed health care startup. Now, he’s reinventing himself once again, this time as a product entrepreneur —and it has him more excited than ever. “My hobbies tend to be learning something new,” Brown told Fortune in a recent interview. “I think I never want to retire,” he added. “Why would you do that? You spent all this time learning something—and things get easier for you when you get older in some ways because you’re a little bit wiser.” His latest experiment is Poka Snack, a skewer-like product designed to make it easier to freeze and eat fruit, particularly bananas. Earlier this year, Brown launched it on Kickstarter, where it has raised more than 90% of its initial $4,000 goal, and he’s already amassed more than 14,000 TikTok followers . But for Brown, the venture is more than a frozen skewer business. It’s another opportunity to step outside his comfort zone, learn something unfamiliar, and find the energy that comes with starting over . “It’s almost like being in college again,” Brown said. “You have that adrenaline flowing. You want to accomplish something.” Don’t be afraid to ‘look stupid’ and take risks, Brown says Brown graduated from the University of Michigan’s medical school in 1980 and spent the next two decades in private practice. In 2004, he returned to his alma mater as a professor, while also serving as director of clinical nuclear medicine and molecular imaging in the university’s division of nuclear medicine. He retired from Michigan in 2020. By then, Brown had spent decades building a career; he could have stepped away and looked back on the patients he treated, the students he taught, and the hefty salary that came with it. Instead, the following Monday he started a new job. Brown became the first vice chair of clinical operations at the University of Utah School of Medicine’s department of radiology, a role he held for three years before joining Covera Health, a venture-backed health-tech startup. Today, he serves as the company’s chief health strategy officer. Still working years after the typical retirement age , constant change and sense of growth is what keeps Brown engaged. Early in a career, he said, much of the work is about learning; eventually, as the job becomes familiar, it can become easier to stop pushing yourself into unfamiliar territory. “When something becomes routine, you probably have stopped growing,” he said. That philosophy has shaped Brown’s relationship with entrepreneurship. During the dot-com boom—while still practicing medicine—he launched several internet ventures, including websites that sold college textbooks and hotel rooms around the world. He also created an educational website for cancer patients and their families. While the era’s bust eventually brought most of those ventures to an end, Brown said the experience taught him not to let the fear of failure—or looking foolish—get in the way. “I think the problem with most people is they’re afraid to look stupid,” Brown said. “If you think that something should be done, just do it. Don’t worry about what other people think, because you may be wrong, but you also may be right. And if you’re right, do you really want to miss that opportunity?” He’s continued to embrace that mindset with Poka Snack, which was inspired by the fact that while he liked eating frozen bananas, existing products were difficult to insert, sometimes broke and could leave splinters in the fruit. “I wanted something better,” Brown said. “When I couldn’t find what I was looking for, I decided to see if I could create it myself.” After testing roughly 40 prototypes, Brown settled on the final design, featuring patent-pending semi-helical geometry. He’s now working with a U.S. manufacturer on production while finalizing the packaging. How a baby boomer used AI to become a ‘solopreneur’ Brown’s latest venture has also given him a crash course in something else: using AI to build a business largely on his own. He’s used the technology throughout the entire Poka Snack development process, from product concept and design to branding, creative work, marketing, his business plan, and the launch. Without it, he said, becoming a “solopreneur” would not have been possible. An AI-generated Poka Snack concept rendering shared with Fortune. But the experience has also reinforced a lesson Brown has learned throughout his career: Instead of worrying about finding the perfect career path, pay attention to what genuinely interests you. “People are always asking: ‘What should I go into?’ and that’s the wrong question,” Brown said. “The question is: ‘What are you excited about?'” It’s a simple philosophy, but one Brown has spent his career putting into practice: Never stop learning or experimenting—and don’t be afraid to start over. events.title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
events.summary: Watch: Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey calls for immediate action on fuel costs Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living. The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January. Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze , deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year. The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump. Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy. "Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said. The policy would cost about £2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding." In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from £3 to £1, and reduce rail fares by 10%. He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair. Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs. Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already. "Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them." events.title: I make up to $15,000 a month online answering appliance questions. I love the flexibility.
events.summary: Matthew Rankin turned his side hustle online into his main job after burning out at his 9-to-5. Photo courtesy of Matthew Morrison Appliance technician Matthew Rankin quit his full-time job and went all in with his side hustle. He now works nine to 10 hours a day answering questions online for JustAnswer. The job can be hectic, but it is flexible and has allowed him to make up to $15,000 a month. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Matthew Rankin, a 52-year-old appliance technician based in Greenville, South Carolina. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I wasn't happy with my work and was getting burned out . I've been an appliance expert for easily 25 years, specializing in dishwashers, refrigerators, and other appliances. Maintenance in general is hard, but when you get into commercial properties and apartment maintenance, it's a whole other league. I worked in commercial property management for about six years, managing facilities and fixing whatever was broken. It wasn't the most glamorous job; you're always on call. After doing that, I decided I would never be on call again. I was looking for an opportunity to make more money on the side I was living in Charleston, South Carolina; it's an expensive region, and I didn't have much in savings. I think I saw a reel on Instagram about JustAnswer , and it looked too good to be true. I was hesitant at first, but I applied and figured I'd give it a couple of hours a day. I'd log on to my computer and close out five or 10 calls or questions. I started seeing these part-time paychecks come in and saw the potential after doing the math, so I decided to go for it. I was in a position that had a lot of flexibility. After about six months, I gave my two-week notice and haven't looked back. Now I make between $10,000 and $15,000 a month answering questions online. How I make money answering questions online When a question comes in, I can accept it or pass it, so it's important to filter them properly. Sometimes the question is about a brand I've never heard of, or a product or situation I'm not familiar with. Questions from other countries pop up every once in a while, too. On JustAnswer, I may get a lot of refrigerator-not-cooling inquiries, and if it's a brand I know — LG, Kenmore, etc. — that's a question I'll take . A lot of the people reaching out are DIYers, newer technicians in the field, or people who simply want access to someone with expertise. They're looking for guidance and help working through the troubleshooting process. I gather as much information as I can quickly: the model number, whether I'll need to look up a part, and anything else I can quickly check on a second screen. 25 to 30 calls in a day is pretty good I can stay on text or be available for a phone call. I've made 50 calls in one day. It's not very common, but it's hectic. I've had phone calls up to an hour, although rare. As for text questions, they can take days, which isn't the goal and is also uncommon. Sometimes the questions come in really fast, and I multitask with 10 windows open, five browsers, and the phone going at the same time. It takes a certain kind of person to be able to balance all of that. The hours are flexible . I tend to stick to 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, but if I do something in the middle of the day, I might work a little later. Nine or 10 hours is probably average, but I'm not sitting in front of the computer working the entire time. If questions aren't coming in, I might play video games or play my guitar in the same room while I wait. Some cons of working online and answering questions all day are that you need to be disciplined and treat it like a 9-to-5 , or you won't make the call load and will keep dropping pay rates. Some days, calls can be sparse; you never know. You hope for the best, make yourself available, and be ready. I have no regrets about leaving my full-time job early — not a single one Something I wish I'd known sooner is to plan for your end-of-year taxes and set aside about 25% of each paycheck. Otherwise, I have no regrets. My last job had no opportunity for advancement and would wear me down both physically and mentally. Advice I'd give someone looking to make a side hustle a full-time job: find something you are really good at and enjoy; the two will connect into something of value. I fell into this incredible opportunity, and it's been life-changing. I've taken full advantage of it, and I do very well. It's not for everyone, but for people who value flexibility and want more balance, it can be a great fit. Do you have an interesting side hustle to share with Business Insider? events.title: The Airbus A380 got a second life. Here's where you can still fly on the world's largest passenger jet.
events.summary: Emirates is the biggest operator of the world's largest passenger jet. Bloomberg/Getty Images Several airlines ditched the Airbus A380 during the pandemic. But it's still flying high, led by Emirates' fleet of 117 superjumbos. Business Insider compiled a list of every airline operating the A380 and their winter routes for 2026. Do you fancy flying on the world's largest passenger jet ? The Airbus A380 has awed passengers for nearly 20 years. With a 262-foot wingspan, the superjumbo jet wouldn't fit on an NFL field. Business Insider has compiled all the routes that it will fly this winter, based on Cirium data for November's schedule. You can search for different cities in this table, then scroll down for more details about the airlines operating the A380. Airbus spent decades developing the double-decker airplane as an answer to the Boeing 747 . It announced the project in 1990, but the A380 didn't enter service until 2007. It has had a turbulent life ever since, falling in and out of popularity. The European planemaker expected high demand for enormous aircraft due to the rise of airport megahubs like Dubai. It was ideal for Emirates, which operates the overwhelming majority of A380s. However, many airlines preferred to fly point-to-point. Twin-jet aircraft like the Boeing 777 and Airbus A350 offer plenty of seats, greater flexibility, and lower operating costs. The COVID-19 pandemic also prompted many airlines to rethink their strategies amid cost pressures. Air France and Malaysia Airlines were among those to retire all their A380s. Airbus built the last new A380 in 2021. While COVID was a major blow, many airlines fell back in love with the superjumbo when lockdowns lifted. Lufthansa retired all 14 of its A380s during the pandemic but has brought back eight of them since 2022. Etihad Airways reactivated six jets, too. Meanwhile, Qantas restarted A380 flights between Sydney and Dallas/Fort Worth last August, for the first time since the pandemic. A year later, though, the Australian flag carrier said it was bringing forward its retirement of the planes to 2028. Back in 2017, there were more than 10,000 flights a month operated by the A380. While that has since fallen to 7,500 for November, it seems there is still some life left in the superjumbo. 1. Emirates Emirates' A380s have a bar onboard. Bloomberg/Getty Images Dubai's airline is by far the world's largest operator of the A380, with over nine times as many as any other operator. Emirates has a total of 117, of which 85 are actively flying as of September, according to fleet data from ch-aviation. 13 are in storage, and 19 are undergoing maintenance. Like its rival Middle Eastern airlines, Emirates' A380 is highly luxurious — with business-class passengers able to visit the bar or even book a shower. The airline's president, Tim Clark, told Business Insider last year that he'd like Airbus to build a new version of the A380 with more fuel-efficient engines. Emirates' plethora of planes comes with a similarly broad route map. Brace yourself for an extensive list. Emirates flies the A380 between Dubai and Amman, Jordan; Amsterdam; Auckland, New Zealand; Bangkok; Barcelona; Bengaluru, India; Birmingham, England; Brisbane, Australia; Cairo; Casablanca, Morocco; Copenhagen, Denmark; Denpasar, Indonesia; Düsseldorf, Germany; Frankfurt, Germany; Glasgow, Scotland; Guangzhou, China; Hong Kong; Houston; Istanbul; Jeddah, Saudi Arabia; Johannesburg; Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia; London; Los Angeles; Madrid; Manchester, England; Mauritius; Melbourne, Australia; Milan; Moscow; Mumbai, India; Munich; New Delhi; New York; Nice, France; Osaka, Japan; Paris; Perth, Australia; Prague; Rome; San Francisco; São Paulo; Seoul; Shanghai; Singapore; Sydney; Taipei; Tokyo; Toronto; Vienna; Washington, DC; and Zurich. Emirates also operates three fifth-freedom flights with the A380, between Christchurch, New Zealand, and Sydney; Bangkok and Hong Kong; and Milan and New York. 2. British Airways British Airways is retrofitting a new first-class suite for the A380. Pete Syme/Business Insider British Airways has 12 Airbus A380s. According to ch-aviation, two of those are undergoing maintenance, and another is in storage, as of September. As part of a $9 billion "transformation program," BA is retrofitting its A380s with an upgraded first class. "The A380 is an important part of our fleet and rightfully, incredibly popular with our customers," Neil Chernoff, BA's chief planning and strategy officer, previously told Business Insider. BA flies the A380 between London Heathrow and Johannesburg, Miami, San Francisco, and Singapore 3. Singapore Airlines A first-class suite on a Singapore Airlines A380. ROSLAN RAHMAN/AFP via Getty Images Singapore Airlines also has a fleet of 12 double-decker jets, having retired seven due to the pandemic. The carrier is one of just 10 to receive a five-star rating from Skytrax. It named Singapore Airlines' business class the second-best, behind Qatar Airways, but the best for first class. The airline offers enormous suites on its A380s, each with an armchair and a bed. Two of these can also be uniquely combined to create a double bed. Singapore flies the A380 between Singapore Changi Airport and Auckland, London, Melbourne, Mumbai, New Delhi, Shanghai, and Sydney. 4. Qatar Airways A Qatar Airways Airbus A380. Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto via Getty Images Qatar Airways cleaned up at last year's Skytrax awards, winning both best airline and best business class. Like Emirates, the airline's A380 includes a bar for business-class passengers. It also has huge bathrooms, but lacks showers. Qatar's A380s, perhaps surprisingly, don't feature its flagship business-class product, the QSuite, which you'll find on the A350, Boeing 777, and 787. Following delays to the Boeing 777X , Qatar reversed plans to retire the A380. Its former CEO, Akbar Al-Bakar, said in 2021 that buying the planes was a "big mistake," given their high operating costs. However, on the sidelines of 2024's Farnborough Airshow, his successor Badr Mohammed Al-Meer — who has since left the CEO position — said the quad-engine was getting a new lease of life. Qatar has eight A380s, which it operates between Doha and Bangkok, London, and Paris. 5. Qantas A Qantas Airbus A380. Sebastian Kahnert/Getty Images Australian flag carrier Qantas has 10 A380s. It flies them from Sydney to Dallas/Fort Worth, Johannesburg, Los Angeles, and Singapore — from which it also continues to London. Plus, the A380 is sometimes used on flights from Melbourne to Los Angeles. A severe storm warning and "incredibly high" demand during Taylor Swift's Australian tour last year saw Qantas use a spare A380 to fly Swifties from Melbourne to Sydney. 6. events.title: Family shares hidden cost of cancer care
events.summary: The family of Maya, 13, from Hythe, say they have faced an increased financial burden while they care for her after she was diagnosed with neuroblastoma The parents of a teenage girl with a rare form of childhood cancer say the hidden costs of caring for their daughter have left them in fear of losing their home. Maya, 13, from Hythe in Kent, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma at three years old, but relapsed in 2023 having been in remission for five years. Her mother, Dellanie, said the pressure of paying a mortgage and bills whilst she and her husband, Terry, are working less to care for Maya is continuing to take its toll on their family of five. Dellanie, an NHS nurse, said: "Whilst your child is poorly and you are fighting for her life, the bills don't stop coming." She added: "My husband has lost his income as he is caring for Maya, and these days you need two people working just to keep your head above water. "It has been very, very difficult but our aim has always been to to look after our child as well as each other. "I always put a brave face on - of course I'm hurting, but I can't be in the corner crying." Maya, who her mother described as a "larger than life person" who loves animals and music, was first diagnosed with neuroblastoma near her adrenal gland when she was three-years-old. Dellanie says Maya is a "larger than life person" who loves animals and music Neuroblastoma is a rare cancer which mainly affects children under five-years-old and around 100 children are diagnosed with it a year in the UK, according to Cancer Research UK. After initially going into remission, Maya's neuroblastoma returned three years ago, and has since been cared for by specialist teams including at the Royal Marsden hospital in London, and Great Ormond Street Hospital. In 2025, during a clinical trial of CAR T-cell therapy, a technique currently used to treat some types of leukaemia and lymphoma, Maya developed a brain injury which Dellanie said left her "profoundly disabled". Her disability meant Terry had to leave his job to care for Maya full time, while Dellanie reduced her working hours to care for her, and support her husband. Dellanie said: "I just have to be grateful for what we have got. "At the moment, Maya is a fighter and there is so much fight in her." Charity Young Lives vs Cancer says families of children with cancer face average extra costs of around £700 a month, and an average loss of income of about £6,000 per household. Sonia Malik, the charity's associate policy director, said: "We find people are having to dip into savings, and most of these costs are immediate. "It impacts the whole family and their lives are thrown into chaos. "The financial stress should be the last thing families have to think about." Malik said that some support is available for cancer patients and their carers, such as financial support from charities, disability benefits and carer's allowance, but it can take time for families to receive benefits support. events.title: I raised my daughter to value making a difference over making money. Now I question that lesson.
events.summary: The author (right) and her daughter both founded nonprofits. Courtesy of Miriam Bonilla. My daughter and I both run nonprofits: mine rescues dogs; hers supports women's education. We are both passionate about our philanthropic work, but it comes at a price. I sometimes wonder if I should have encouraged her to choose a paycheck over passion and purpose. Two years ago, my daughter, Jordan, was in the outskirts of Marrakech in Morocco with a group of 15 Amazigh girls from the High Atlas Mountains . Displaced after a recent earthquake, they were in a temporary dorm, just a small house, but it was all they had available to them. My daughter was leading a yoga teacher training program through her nonprofit — one that she built herself from the ground up when she was 26. "How hot is it?" I ask while sitting at my desk in Los Angeles, frantically putting together a fundraising plea for the charity I founded for a matted poodle mix with a broken leg. He was hit by a car, and one of our rescue volunteers just saved him and rushed him to our vets. "44 Celsius, Mom, and no fans. Cell phone cutting out," she shares. I quickly Google the Fahrenheit conversion and learn that it's about 111 degrees. "Oh no!" I gasp. "Texting you Hamza's number. Nice guy. He'll help," she says. "On it!" I yell, but she's gone. This is the path my daughter and I have chosen. We are both founders of our own nonprofits . Our roller coaster lives are filled with daily problem-solving and never-ending stress. I'm proud of the person my daughter has become, but now I sometimes wonder if I should have pushed her in a different direction. I'm always ready to help It was a cool 69 degrees where I was in Santa Monica, yet my whole body suddenly felt blazing hot. As mothers, we are always split in two, immersed in our own lives, but also wherever our children are, even if it's on the other side of the world . Within an hour of connecting with my daughter, I reached Hamza in Marrakesh, arranged for six large fans to be delivered C.O.D. by morning, and am laser-focused on raising $4,200 needed for the emergency pup who's already in surgery. Do you have a parenting regret? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. That night, as I feed my current pack of rescue dogs , I ask myself the push-pull, ever-pervasive question: Should I have encouraged my daughter to choose something more stable and secure, but less noble? I was raised in apartheid South Africa. My parents left with their three daughters, without trying to change a system they hated. As a young adult in America, I suffered from terrible guilt. Why did we just walk away? I wanted to model something different for my daughter "Make a difference. Leave a footprint on the planet. Care about others," was the mantra I later instilled in my only child as a single mother. At the age of 9, Jordan, already passionate about causes, went off to protest to save spider monkeys, picketing with a sign. When she was a teenager, I started rescuing dogs. Having always been a huge animal lover, all it took was saving one little Chihuahua to open my eyes to the plight of animals in need. My daughter saw how dramatically my life changed. Heels were replaced by flip-flops, hair appointments were sacrificed for vet visits, and gradually, mutts took the place of men. By the time she left for college, I had started my own dog rescue foundation. My daughter often puts others first My examples seemed to stick with her. During her sophomore year, Jordan studied abroad in Cambodia and volunteered at a school teaching English. It lit a fire that was already smoldering in her. At 26, she founded Souljourn Yoga Foundation, raising funds for young women's education globally through ethical yoga retreats and partnering with NGOs on the ground. Now, over a decade later, I've witnessed the joys but also the struggles she's experienced, many of which mirror my own. How do we get more donors? Will that grant proposal be approved? Can we make it through the fiscal year? I lie awake at night and angst for us both. I have mixed feelings now People often say to us, "Thank goodness for angels like you!" But they don't see the personal sacrifices behind those words. There's the three major back surgeries I've had from lifting large dogs and heavy bags of food, and the five hours of sleep Jordan and I both average a night, consumed by our missions that neither of us can switch off, holding up our own heavens like Atlas, as it were. But there are also nights when I lie in bed and cherish the magic moments. The 23 hours of air travel I took to hear the infectious, gleeful laughter of schoolchildren in Hikkaduwa, Sri Lanka, as they stretched their arms high in a yoga posture they had never done before. The glow I felt watching my daughter lead them, encouraging them to reach for the sky. And recently, I received a text from the adopter of that injured poodle-mix we named Romeo. He's now a healthy, fluffy, racing-around pup who is loved and adored. These are the riches that cannot be counted in dollars or measured by a bank balance. Yet, with rising costs, declining funding , and the future of many small nonprofits uncertain, I grapple daily with the question as her mother: Should I have encouraged my daughter to choose a paycheck over passion and purpose? These days, I'm not so sure I know the answer. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: UK minister warns of impact of Trump’s Iran war on next month’s budget
events.summary: Bridget Phillipson says Burnham’s past criticisms of US president not an issue as PM prepares to meet Trump at UN Next month’s budget will be made more difficult by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, one of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said, while adding she did not expect the prime minister’s previous disparaging comments about the US president to be an issue. Burnham is expected to meet Trump early next week at the UN general assembly summit in New York, the pair having previously spoken twice by phone since Burnham entered No 10. As Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham said Trump would not be welcome in the city, saying also that UK politicians who indulged him “should be ashamed”. Asked about the comments, Bridget Phillipson , the Labour chair and minister for women and equalities, told Sky News: “Look, I think what you’ve just described there is politics. The president knows that. This is far from unique. “People will express views at different points on different topics. And that’s no bar to having a strong relationship.” She nonetheless repeated UK condemnation of Trump’s on-and-off military campaign against Iran, which has disrupted global oil supplies, causing significant inflationary pressures , saying this would make life more difficult for John Healey, the chancellor, as he plans the budget. The economy was, Phillipson said, “in a strong position”, especially with growth figures. She said: “But that’s not to take away from the very real challenges that you identify, particularly where it’s come to the conflict we’ve seen in the Middle East and the impact that that’s been having on businesses and on families close to home. “We took the decision not to involve ourselves in that conflict. That was the right call. The US will take their own foreign policy decisions, but I believe, and still believe now, it was the right decision for us as a country not to get involved in that conflict. Of course, something that, had Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage been running the country, we would have jumped headlong into a conflict with it without end. “And yet, and we do see the consequences here at home and as we go into the budget, making sure that we are doing everything we can to give people that breathing space to tackle those challenges around the cost of living has been at the forefront of everything that Andy Burnham has done since becoming prime minister. “I know it’s at the forefront of the chancellor’s mind as he’s planning for that budget later on next month.” Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters In a later interview with the BBC, Phillipson was dismissive of comments by Jim Ratcliffe, the petrochemicals billionaire, who said this week he had lost confidence in the UK due to levels of immigration and taxation. She said: “You’ll forgive me if I do take with a pinch of salt what someone who is a tax exile has to say about our country.” Ratcliffe is resident for tax in Monaco. Burnham has previously defended his comments about Trump in a similar way, saying of the US president: “Well, he’s said things as well, and everyone says things as politicians. In the moment, you meet people where they’re at, and you find a connection with people, and that’s always been my style.” With the wider UK-US relationship, there were “differences of opinion”, Phillipson said, while arguing that Burnham could see beyond those differences with Trump in maintaining invaluable ties. She said: “We don’t have the same political outlook, but the relationship between the UK and the US goes beyond any one president, any one prime minister. “It’s something that has stood the test of time over many centuries, despite political differences. They come and go. What matters most is the British national interest. And that’s what Andy Burnham will deliver for our country.”
